# Ezekiel 11: research notes, verse by verse

**What these notes cover.** I used up my search and page-reading allowance before I could find anything on the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey, the netbible.org notes themselves, or prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out. The only Catholic voice below is Haydock's commentary as it appears on StudyLight. I also didn't find a clear split between Protestant denominations on any verse. Where the commentators disagree, the disagreement is about how to read the text, not along church lines. I've marked those places and noted each writer's tradition where the site gives it.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik says this carries on the vision that began in chapter 8. Ezekiel was bodily still in Babylon, but God showed him Jerusalem's spiritual corruption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- Guzik also notes that this Jaazaniah has a different father from the one in 8:9-11, so he seems to be a different man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- Precept Austin says most (but not all) commentators think these 25 are not the sun-worshippers of 8:16. Those were probably priests, while these are called "leaders of the people," stand at a different spot, and are charged with bad leadership rather than false worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_111-12
- Coffman takes all 25 to be government and civil leaders. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ezekiel-11.html

**v. 2:** Pulpit/Keil note that nothing more is known of the two named men. The charge of giving evil counsel fits civil rulers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-3.htm

**v. 3 (a debated verse):**
- *Question or statement?* The ESV Study Bible says the wicked counsel quoted here is obscure. If 3a is a statement, the pot-and-meat picture is negative ("we're cooked!"). If it is a question, it is positive ("we won't be burned!"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_111-12 Guzik prefers the question: "Isn't it time to build houses?" He reads it as confidence that Jerusalem would be safe from Babylon, just as meat is safe in a covered pot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *Most common reading:* The Pulpit Commentary paraphrases it as: let us build houses here, not in exile as Jeremiah urged, because the pot shields the meat from the fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-3.htm
- Wiersbe (quoted by Guzik) adds a jibe: the leaders saw themselves as choice cuts and the exiles as scraps. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *A reference to Jeremiah?* Jamieson-Fausset-Brown thinks the leaders were mocking Jeremiah 1:13, where the city is pictured as a boiling pot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-3.htm Keil & Delitzsch disagree. They say the words have nothing in common with that picture in Jeremiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-11.html
- *A different line:* Clarke reads it as stubborn defiance: we will stay and share the city's fate even if it perishes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-3.html
- *Catholic reading:* The Douay-Rheims follows the Septuagint here, translating "Were not houses lately built?" https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/11-3.htm Haydock takes the point to be that newly built houses proved the city would not be destroyed, against what the prophets were saying. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-3.html
- *Where the summaries disagree:* StudyLight says its commentators split six ways on this verse. Its labels put JFB with the Calvinists and Wesley with the Arminians. The split is about the obscure wording, not about doctrine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-3.html

**v. 4:** Guzik takes this as God's direct order to prophesy against the leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/

**vv. 5–6:** Guzik says God knew the leaders' thoughts, not only their deeds. The words "you have multiplied your slain" put the responsibility for the coming judgment on them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the slain include people the leaders killed outright and people who died because their policies brought the Babylonian army. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-3.html

**v. 7:** Keil says Ezekiel hands their own words back to them. The words are true, but not in the sense they meant: the murdered are the meat in the pot. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-11.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical calls it grim satire: only the dead are "safe" in the pot. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-3.html
- Coffman says the victims, not the leaders, are the true elite of the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ezekiel-11.html
- The Reformation Study Bible agrees that the slain are the "best part." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_111-12

**vv. 8–10:** Benson (Wesleyan) says they feared the Babylonian sword and courted Babylon's favour to avoid it, giving up God's worship for idolatry, yet that same sword would come on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-10.html
- Wesley's note on v. 10: God's judgments would follow them wherever they ran. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-10.html
- "The borders of Israel" is identified as Riblah by Trapp (cited by Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/ Wesley says the same, adding that the captive king saw his children killed there before his eyes were put out. https://www.ccel.org/w/wesley/notes/notes/Ezekiel.html
- Guzik says God would keep dealing with his people even after Jerusalem fell. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/

**v. 11:** Gill: the city was a pot for the dead, not for the living. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-11.html
- Chuck Smith: it would not save them from Babylon's fire. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-11.html
- Coffman: everyone who survived would be deported. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-11.html

**v. 12:** Guzik says that since Israel copied the nations, it was fitting for God to exile them among the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- The Biblical Illustrator applies this as a warning to leaders who conform to the world. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-11.html

**v. 13:** Precept Austin says Pelatiah's death confirmed Ezekiel's message and gave a foretaste of judgment on the other leaders. His name means something like "Yahweh delivers," which is ironic. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1113-25
- Coffman says Pelatiah died in Jerusalem at the very moment Ezekiel saw it in the vision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/ezekiel-11.html
- The Pulpit Commentary compares the death of the false prophet Hananiah in Jeremiah 28. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/11-3.htm
- Guzik says Ezekiel's cry echoes 9:8: he was stunned and wondered whether anyone would survive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/

**v. 14:** Precept Austin calls God's answer the first promise of restoration in Ezekiel and roots it in the covenant with Abraham. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1113-25

**v. 15:** Precept Austin says the people of Jerusalem assumed God's power was limited to his land, and that v. 16 refutes this. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1113-25
- MacArthur (quoted by Precept Austin) says Ezekiel's real family was now his fellow exiles, not the Jerusalem priests he was related to by blood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1113-25
- The Restoration Commentary says the exiles, far from being outcasts, had become the true Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/ezekiel-11.html

**v. 16 (a debated verse: what does "little" mean?):**
- *"For a little while."* Ellicott says the word is an adverb and could mean time or amount, but the context points to time: during the captivity, God's presence would stand in for the Temple. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/11-16.htm Barnes (Presbyterian) and the Pulpit Commentary read it the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-16.html Feinberg (via Guzik) says "little sanctuary" could never be true of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *"Small."* Wesley takes it as a little temple set against the great one in Jerusalem. In exile they would have the kind of communion with God once thought possible only in the Temple. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-ezekiel/ Spurgeon (Baptist) reads "little" as God lowering himself to each believer's smallness: a sanctuary that is near and suited to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-16.html
- *Other readings.* Gill cites Jewish interpreters (the Targum, Rashi, Kimchi) who applied the verse to synagogues in exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-16.htm Matthew Henry: Jerusalem had the temple without God, and Babylon had God without the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-15.html Block (via Guzik) calls the statement without parallel in the Old Testament. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *Dispensational application:* Chuck Smith says it explains why the Jews kept their identity through the worldwide dispersion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-16.html
- *Possible Catholic variant:* The New American Bible reads "but little sanctuary," which seems to point in a different direction. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/11-16.htm

**v. 17:** Guzik says the restoration is as sure as the judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *A point of disagreement:* Feinberg (dispensational, via Guzik) argues that God never cancelled this land grant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/ The Restoration Commentary instead stresses the exiles as "the true Israel." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/ezekiel-11.html

**v. 18:** Guzik says the exile was a time of cleansing, and that after it Israel did not struggle with idols the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- Clarke (Methodist) says the same: they would put away all idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-16.html

**v. 19:** Guzik ties this to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 37. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-11/
- *God's work alone.* Gill: only God can remove the stony heart; people cannot soften their own hearts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/ezekiel/11-19.html JFB: God calls it his free gift so that the people cannot claim credit for v. 18. The Geneva notes speak of God regenerating them anew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-19.htm
- *Wesleyan emphasis.* Clarke (Methodist) describes the change as "a whole system of renewed affections." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-19.html
- *Regeneration and conversion.* The Biblical Illustrator says regeneration is God's change in the heart, while conversion is the person turning his own life. Both should be held, each in its place. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-11.html
- *New Testament links.* Coffman connects the verse to Jesus' talk with Nicodemus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-19.html The Pulpit Commentary calls the idea the same as Jeremiah 31:31-33. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-19.htm

**v. 20:** The Biblical Illustrator: practice must follow principle; the effect shows the cause. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/ezekiel-11.html

**v. 21:** I found no comment on this verse.

**v. 22:** Keil says the glory had already left the temple. Now it leaves the city too, a sign that neither was the seat of God's gracious presence any longer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-23.htm

**v. 23:**
- *The mountain.* Commentators agree it is the Mount of Olives. Benson (Wesleyan) and Clarke see God's patience in a departure made step by step. Clarke lists four stages, ending with the glory going to heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-23.html
- *Waiting for repentance, or waiting to judge?* Gill holds both possibilities open. Keil says the glory stayed there to carry out the judgment. Barnes records a rabbinic tradition that the Shekinah called the people to repent from that mountain for three years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-23.htm
- *Christ.* Matthew Henry sees it as a picture of Christ's ascension from that same mountain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/11-23.htm Chuck Smith (dispensational) links it to Christ's return there (Zechariah 14:4). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-23.html
- TGC's devotional: God's presence leaves temple and city as an act of judgment, and nothing now stands in the way of their destruction. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/2-samuel-2-1-corinthians-13-ezekiel-11-psalm-50/
- Guzik (via a quotation he cites) notes that Ezekiel does not say whether the glory went further than the mountain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Eze/Eze-11.cfm

**vv. 24–25:** Ellicott says the vision ends and Ezekiel returns in spirit to Chaldea. There he shows the exiles that trusting in the guilty city's survival is futile. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/11-23.htm
- Henry: seeing the glory rise out of sight confirmed that the vision came from heaven. Glimpses of glory like this are not constant in this life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/11-23.html
